title: UnitedHealth Just Proved Warren Buffett Right -- Again
content:
Investors are seeing why Buffett earned the nickname "the Oracle of Omaha."
Flashback to the second quarter of last year. The wheels seemed to be coming off for UnitedHealth Group (UNH 0.10%). The healthcare giant first revised its full-year outlook downward, then yanked the guidance altogether. Its CEO was shown the exit door. Reports surfaced about an investigation by the U.S. Department of Justice. UnitedHealth's stock was sinking fast.
But there was at least one major investor who wasn't worried. Warren Buffett initiated a $1.6 billion stake in the health insurance stock for Berkshire Hathaway's (BRKA 0.28%) (BRKB 0.27%) portfolio. Buffett saw an overreaction related to temporary issues facing a company that remained fundamentally strong.
Now, let's return to the present. UnitedHealth Group reported its first-quarter results on Wednesday. And the investing world got to see why Buffett earned the nickname "the Oracle of Omaha." UnitedHealth proved Buffett right -- again. 
Image source: The Motley Fool.
Berkshire Hathaway is a leader in the property & casualty (P&C) insurance market. Although P&C is different from health insurance, Buffett knew of one common denominator: when insurers' bottom lines suffer, they can nearly always raise rates to fix the problem.

title: Molina controls costs in Q1 but future Medicaid spending in doubt
content:
Let Healthcare Dive’s free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.
                    
                
            
The insurer beat analyst expectations for adjusted earnings in the first quarter. But steeper Medicaid membership losses than expected could saddle Molina with higher costs.
Molina benefited from better controlled Medicaid spending in the first quarter, though steeper membership losses than expected raise questions about whether the insurer can keep costs in hand for the remainder of 2026.
Molina posted better-than-expected first quarter earnings on Wednesday afternoon, sending the insurer’s stock up more than 10% in Thursday morning’s trade.
Yet, unlike its peers UnitedHealth and Elevance, which both raised 2026 guidance after keeping medical spending in check, Molina elected to reaffirm its outlook.
Executives said retaining the current 2026 guidance is prudent given it’s early in the year and the cost environment remains challenging. Still, they hinted Molina might update the outlook after the second quarter.
But a lot remains up in the air despite Molina’s relatively buoyant start to 2026.
The Trump administration’s efforts to curtail what it views as overly permissive Medicaid enrollment, especially for undocumented immigrants, have caused Molina to lose more Medicaid members than expected.
That membership decline could coincide with an increase in spending if the members who remain are sicker than those who left — a worry Molina executives attempted to convince investors was overblown on a Thursday morning call.
Washington is also creating challenges for Molina’s Affordable Care Act plans, while Molina’s decision to prune its underperforming Medicare Advantage business is also eating into the company’s bottom line.
Overall, Molina brought in just $14 million in profit in the quarter, compared to a profit of $298 million in the first quarter last year.
Slipping profits reflected higher administrative spending, along with a $93 million impairment charge related to Molina’s planned exit of certain MA plans, according to financial documents.
Molina’s revenue also dipped by 3% year over year to $10.8 billion as membership losses ate into the insurer’s premiums.
Insurers like Molina with a heavy presence in government programs, where they have less direct control over reimbursement, have struggled to contain rising costs as members consume more medical care that becomes more expensive.

Molina’s dour earnings outlook illustrates that insurers think it’ll remain difficult to turn a profit in programs like Medicaid and the ACA this year.

title: Why BSX Stock's Q1 Beat Is A Lagging Indicator
content:
The primary insight within Boston Scientific’s (BSX) Q1 2026 results is that the adjusted EPS beat of $0.80 acts as a lagging indicator, contrasting with a moderating trend in forward-looking growth. While management maintained a 28.0% operating margin, the decision to revise full-year 2026 organic revenue guidance from a 10%–11% range to 6.5%–8.0% is the critical signal for investors. This dynamic highlights a strategic divergence from other healthcare leaders. For instance, while our analysis of How UNH Stock Is Trading Short-Term Margins For Long-Term Moats details a deliberate sacrifice of current profitability to fortify competitive positioning, Boston Scientific is preserving current margins even as its primary growth engines encounter emerging headwinds.
The guidance revision stems from a “greater than expected market share loss” in the Electrophysiology (EP) segment, specifically within the Pulsed Field Ablation (PFA) market. Boston Scientific’s FARAPULSE system is facing intensified competition from Johnson & Johnson’s (JNJ) Varipulse, which is natively integrated into the dominant CARTO mapping platform. This platform integration creates a competitive advantage in clinical workflows that BSX has yet to fully address with its current ecosystem. This strategic challenge stands in contrast to the recent performance of Intuitive Surgical (See How ISRG Just Secured The U.S. Market), where a dominant and integrated install base provides a level of market insulation that Boston Scientific is currently working to replicate in the competitive PFA landscape.
The Cardiovascular segment represents approximately 67% of total company revenue. While it reported 11.2% organic growth in the first quarter, the revised full-year outlook implies a meaningful deceleration for the remainder of 2026. This trend is compounded by performance challenges in the WATCHMAN and Urology franchises. The 6% year-over-year increase in adjusted EPS was achieved through disciplined cost-cutting and margin control rather than sustained top-line expansion in these high-margin categories. See how BSX’s growth and margins compare to some of its peers, including Medtronic (MDT) and Abbott (ABT).
The investment narrative is transitioning from one of rapid expansion to a focus on defending existing market share. Boston Scientific is now perceived as a firm in transition, working to justify a premium valuation against a backdrop of moderating growth and an evolving competitive landscape. At current levels, the stock trades at approximately $65, implying a multiple of 21 times trailing adjusted earnings. This represents a significant reset from the 32x average seen over the last three years, a premium previously supported by the high-growth trajectories of the WATCHMAN and overall Cardiovascular segment.
